title: Our environment: the living and non-living world around us, and how we care for it

summary.text: Shut a few moong seeds in a clear box with damp cotton and close the lid. No water is added for a week, yet they stay green, while the seeds in an open box dry out. Everything around a living thing is their environment. It has living parts, such as plants, animals, microbes and people, and non-living parts, such as air, water, soil, light and warmth. Some things in it are natural, and some are made by people. All these parts keep changing each other. Earth works like the closed box: sunlight comes in, but the same water and air go round and round, so what we pour or throw out stays in our shared home.
summary.art: Two clear takeaway boxes side by side on a windowsill: the closed one misty with drops and full of green moong sprouts, the open one with dry cotton and drooping sprouts.

intro.hook: Can a plant live inside a closed box, with no new water and no new air? Before you answer, say why you think so. In England, a man named David Latimer planted a bottle garden in 1960. He last watered it in 1972 and closed it with a cork. News reports say the plants were still growing more than forty years later.
intro.text: In this unit you look at everything around you: the living things, the non-living things, and the things people have made. You find out how they change each other. You shut moong seeds in a box and see how they manage. You follow your kitchen water and your rubbish to find where 'away' really is. And you hear about eight people who lived for two years inside a sealed glass building.
intro.art: A large round glass bottle with a cork, full of green plants, on a wooden shelf, with tiny drops on the inside of the glass.

outcomes: I can say what the environment is, and name living and non-living parts of the environment around my home.
I can sort things into natural and made by people, and explain why some things are a bit of both.
I can give examples of how living and non-living parts of the environment change each other.
I can explain, from the closed box test, why the seeds in the closed box kept their water and the open box dried out.
I can explain why Earth is like a closed box: sunlight comes in, but the same water and air go round.
I can follow my kitchen water and my rubbish to where they really go, and suggest a way to send less out.
I can plan and carry out one real way my family can care for the environment, and check whether it worked.

terms.meaning: Everything around a living thing that affects them: air, water, soil, light, warmth, other living things and the things people make.
terms.example: Your environment today includes the air in your room, the fan, the crow at the window and the people at home.
terms.art: A child at a window with labels pointing to the air, a tree, a crow, the sun, a road and a building.

terms.meaning: Something that is alive: they take in food, breathe, grow, make young like themselves, sense and respond, and one day die.
terms.example: A crow, a tulsi plant, an ant and you are all living things.
terms.art: A crow, a tulsi plant in a pot, an ant and a girl in a row.

terms.meaning: Something that is not alive and does not grow, breathe or make young by itself.
terms.example: A stone, the air, water, a steel tumbler and a chair are non-living things.
terms.art: A stone, a glass of water, a steel tumbler and a plastic chair in a row.

terms.meaning: The non-living part of the environment: air, water, soil, rocks, light and warmth, and also buildings and roads.
terms.example: In a Chennai flat, the physical environment includes the hot afternoon air, the tap water and the concrete walls.
terms.art: A flat's balcony with labels for sunlight, air, a water tap, a concrete wall and a pot of soil.

terms.meaning: The living part of the environment: plants, animals, fungi, microbes and people. Books also call it the biological environment.
terms.example: The living environment of a balcony may hold a money plant, ants, a pigeon and the family.
terms.art: A balcony with a money plant, a line of ants, a pigeon on the rail and a family member watering.

terms.meaning: Made by nature, not by people.
terms.example: A river, a rock, a cloud, a coconut and a neem tree are natural.
terms.art: A river with rocks, a coconut palm and clouds above.

terms.meaning: Made by people from natural materials, using their skill and work. Books also say 'man-made' or 'human-made'.
terms.example: A road, a steel tumbler, a plastic bucket and a cotton shirt are made by people.
terms.art: A road, a steel tumbler, a plastic bucket and a folded cotton shirt.

terms.meaning: When a liquid evaporates, it slowly turns into a gas that mixes into the air. Water that evaporates becomes water vapour, which we cannot see.
terms.example: A wet floor dries because its water evaporates into the air.
terms.art: A wet footprint on a tiled floor, fading, with faint dots rising from it.

terms.meaning: When water vapour in the air cools, it condenses: it turns back into tiny drops of liquid water.
terms.example: Drops form on the outside of a cold steel tumbler because water vapour in the air condenses on it.
terms.art: A cold steel tumbler with small drops of water on its outside.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air that people and animals breathe in, and that plants and many microbes use too. Green plants and algae give it out when they make food in light.
terms.example: Every breath you take carries oxygen into your lungs.
terms.art: A child breathing in beside a green plant, with small arrows of air between them.

terms.meaning: A living thing too small to see without a microscope, such as a bacterium or a yeast cell.
terms.example: The bacteria that turn milk into curd are microbes.
terms.art: A bowl of curd with a magnified circle showing tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: Something harmful added to air, water or land, usually by people, in amounts the living things there cannot cope with.
terms.example: Smoke from burning rubbish is air pollution. Soapy water and sewage in a lake is water pollution.
terms.art: A lake with white froth on the water and a drain pipe pouring into it.

explanations.definition: The environment is everything around a living thing that affects them.
explanations.description: Look out of any window and you see part of your environment. It is the air you breathe and the water you drink. It is the sun that warms you, the floor under you and the noise of the road. It is also the crow on the wall, the ants in the kitchen, the people at home and the microbes in your curd. Every living thing has their own environment. An ant's environment is the floor, the crumbs, the other ants and the smell trails they leave. A fish's environment is mostly water. The word comes from an old French word for 'surroundings'.
examples: A pigeon's environment includes the ledge they nest on, the grain people throw and the cats that hunt them.
A tulsi plant's environment includes the pot of soil, the sunlight, the water you pour and the ants that visit.
Your environment at school is different from your environment at home, though you are the same person.
explanations.art: A girl standing at a window in a Madurai flat, with the view labelled: sun, air, neem tree, crow, auto-rickshaw, temple tower.
explanations.context: This card says what the word 'environment' means, with examples from a home in India.

explanations.definition: The environment has a living part (plants, animals, fungi, microbes and people) and a non-living, or physical, part (air, water, soil, rocks, light, warmth, and the things people build).
explanations.description: Books split the environment into two parts. The living part is also called the biological environment. It holds every plant, animal, fungus and microbe, and people too. The non-living part is called the physical environment. It holds air, water, soil, rocks, sunlight and warmth. Buildings, roads and fans are non-living too, so they belong to the physical environment. To decide which part something belongs to, ask: does this grow, breathe and make young like itself? A dry seed is tricky. They look lifeless, but they are alive and will sprout when given water.
examples: Living: the money plant, the gecko on the wall, the bacteria in curd, your grandmother.
Non-living: the tap water, the sunlight on the floor, the concrete wall, the ceiling fan.
Tricky: a dry moong seed is alive, though they seem to do nothing. A wooden door was once part of a living tree, but the door is not alive.
explanations.art: A page split down the middle: on one side a plant, an ant, a bird and a person, on the other side the sun, a glass of water, a stone and a fan.
explanations.context: This card is about the two parts of the environment: the living part and the non-living, or physical, part.

explanations.concept: Natural, made by people, or both
explanations.definition: Natural things are made by nature. Things made by people are made from natural materials using human skill and work.
explanations.description: A river, a cloud and a coconut are natural. A road, a steel tumbler and a plastic bucket are made by people. But everything people make starts as something natural. Steel is made from iron ore dug out of the ground. Plastic is made mostly from oil or gas from deep under the ground. Paper is made from wood. Many things are a bit of both. Curd is made by people, but microbes do the work. A potted tulsi is a natural plant, placed and cared for by people. Many old lakes in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, called eri or kere, were dug and banked by people long ago, and now fish and birds live in them.
examples: Natural: a neem tree, rain, a crow, sand.
Made by people: a bus, a steel plate, a nylon rope, a brick.
Both: curd, a mango tree planted by your grandfather, a temple tank full of fish.
explanations.art: Three boxes: Natural (a cloud, a coconut, a rock), Made by people (a bus, a steel plate, a bucket), Both (a bowl of curd, a potted tulsi, a temple tank with fish).
explanations.context: This card is about telling natural things from things made by people, and about the things that are a bit of both.

explanations.definition: The living and non-living parts of the environment change each other all the time.
explanations.description: The non-living parts decide who can live where. Moss grows in a damp corner, not on a dry, sunny wall. Geckos wait near the tube light, because insects come to the light at night. Living things change the non-living parts too. Plants take water from the soil and give it out through tiny holes in their leaves, into the air. In light, green plants take carbon dioxide from the air and give out oxygen. Earthworms and microbes turn dead leaves into soil. A peepal seed that lands in a crack in a wall can grow roots that split the wall. People change the environment most of all. We build roads and flats, dig lakes, cut forests, plant trees, and send smoke, sewage and rubbish out of our homes.
examples: A moong seedling drinks water from the cotton and gives some of it to the air.
A peepal growing on an old wall slowly breaks the bricks with their roots.
A city built of concrete gets hotter in summer than the green land around it.
explanations.art: A peepal sapling growing out of a crack in an old brick wall, with roots spreading into the cracks.
explanations.context: This card is about how living things and non-living things around us keep changing each other.

explanations.concept: Earth is like a closed box
explanations.definition: Earth gets energy from outside, as sunlight, but almost no new water or air. The same water and air are used again and again.
explanations.description: Remember the closed box test, with moong seeds on damp cotton? In the closed box, water evaporated from the cotton and the leaves, condensed on the cold lid, and ran back down. The water went round inside the box. Earth works the same way. Earth has no lid, but gravity holds the air and water close to Earth. Sunlight comes in from outside, and heat goes back out to space. But almost no new water arrives, and almost none leaves. So the water in your glass has fallen as rain and flowed in rivers many times. It has been inside many plants and animals before you. The oxygen in the air was made by plants, algae and some bacteria, and it is breathed in and given out again and again.
examples: Water you pour down the sink does not disappear. It goes to a drain, a treatment plant, a river, a lake or the sea, and later rises again as water vapour.
Smoke from burning rubbish spreads through the air and comes down with rain, or is breathed in by people far away.
Plastic thrown into a drain can reach the sea and stay there for many years.
explanations.art: Earth seen from space, with a thin blue layer of air, sunlight arriving from one side and small arrows showing water going round between sea, cloud, rain and river.
explanations.context: This card explains why Earth is like the closed box in our experiment: sunlight comes in, but the water and air go round and round.

explanations.definition: When we throw something away or wash it away, it does not leave the Earth. It only goes somewhere else in the environment.
explanations.description: We say 'throw it away' as if 'away' were a place outside the world. It is not. In Chennai, much of the city's rubbish is taken to big dump yards at Kodungaiyur and Perungudi. In Mumbai, much of it goes to Deonar. Waste water from homes flows through drains. Some of it is cleaned at sewage treatment plants, and some flows straight into rivers, lakes or the sea. In Bengaluru, soap and sewage flowing into Bellandur Lake made thick white froth that blew onto the roads. Food peels can rot back into soil, if they are kept apart from plastic. Plastic and glass stay much as they are for a very long time. So caring for the environment starts with asking, 'Where will this go next?'
examples: A banana peel in a compost pot becomes soil in a few weeks.
A plastic wrapper thrown on the road can be washed into a drain by the rain.
Cooking oil poured down a sink can stick inside the pipes and block them.
explanations.art: A kitchen sink with its pipe followed down the side of a building, into a street drain, and on to a lake with froth on it.
explanations.context: This card follows our rubbish and kitchen water to where they really go.

explanations.concept: What helps most when we care for the environment?
explanations.description: Everyone agrees that air, water and land need care. People disagree about what helps most. Some say small changes by every family matter most: carrying a cloth bag, sorting waste, not wasting water. Others say the big changes matter most: how cities treat sewage, how factories work, and how much forest is kept. Many people say both are needed, because big changes start when many people care.
examples: A family in Mysuru sorts their waste into wet and dry, so the wet waste can be composted.
A city builds a sewage treatment plant, so far less dirty water reaches the lake.
Women in Reni village in the Himalayas, led by Gaura Devi, stood around their trees in 1974 to stop them being cut. This was part of the Chipko movement.

perspectives.explanation: Each family's choices add up, because a city is made of families. Small habits, done every day by millions of people, change how much waste and dirty water there is.
Most pollution comes from big sources: cities without sewage treatment, factories, power plants and vehicles. Changing those makes the biggest difference, so laws and city plans matter most.

perspectives.who: People in movements like Chipko and Appiko
perspectives.explanation: Ordinary people acting together can change what governments and companies do. In 1983, villagers near Sirsi in Karnataka hugged trees to stop them being felled. 'Appiko' means 'hug' in Kannada.

explanations.art: A family sorting waste into two bins in their kitchen, and behind them, through the window, a city sewage plant and a green hill.
explanations.context: This card is about a real disagreement: does caring for the environment depend most on what each family does, or on what cities and companies do?

agreed.text: The environment has living parts and non-living parts, and they change each other all the time.
agreed.evidence: We can watch it: plants give water to the air, moss grows only in damp places, and people build, dig and plant.

agreed.text: Earth gets energy from the Sun but almost no new water or air. Water and air go round and round.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measure the water cycle and the air. Only tiny amounts of matter arrive from space as dust and meteorites.

agreed.text: Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by living things.
agreed.evidence: Rocks show that early Earth had almost no oxygen in the air. Oxygen built up after tiny living things in the sea, called cyanobacteria, began making it in sunlight, over two billion years ago.

agreed.text: What we throw out or pour away stays somewhere in the environment.
agreed.evidence: Dump yards, plastic found on beaches and in the sea, and froth on city lakes show where waste ends up.

agreed.text: A closed container with plants, water and light can keep the plants alive for a long time without new water.
agreed.evidence: Bottle gardens and the closed box test both show water going round inside: drops on the lid, then back into the soil or cotton.

challenging.claim: The environment means wild places far away, like forests and the sea, not the city.
challenging.for: Forests and seas have many more wild plants and animals than a city street.
challenging.against: A city flat has an environment too: air, water, light, ants, geckos, pigeons, potted plants and people. City life also depends on rivers, lakes and farms far away.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that only far-away wild places count as 'the environment'.

challenging.claim: Natural things are always good and things made by people are always bad for the environment.
challenging.for: Many things people make, like plastic bags and smoke, do harm, and natural forests and lakes support a lot of life.
challenging.against: Some natural things are harmful, like a snake's venom or a flood. Some made things help, like a sewage treatment plant, a water filter or a bird bath. What matters is what a thing does, not who made it.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that 'natural' means good and 'made by people' means bad.

challenging.claim: One family is far too small to change the environment.
challenging.for: One family's rubbish is a tiny part of a whole city's.
challenging.against: A city is made of families, and habits spread from family to family. Laws such as India's 2022 ban on many single-use plastic items came after many people asked for change.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the choices of one family make any difference.

challenging.claim: Biosphere 2 showed that people can never build a working closed world.
challenging.who: Some writers after the first Biosphere 2 mission
challenging.for: The oxygen fell so low that fresh oxygen had to be pumped in, and many plants and animals died out.
challenging.against: The mission taught scientists exactly why the oxygen fell: rich soil full of microbes and fresh concrete. Small closed worlds, like bottle gardens, can run for decades. Space agencies still study closed life-support systems.
challenging.context: This card is about Biosphere 2, a large sealed glass building in the USA, and what it really showed.

big_questions.q: The water in your closed box went from cotton to air to lid and back again. Is the water in your body part of you, or part of the environment passing through?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the water in you came from this morning, and where it goes when you breathe out or sweat.

big_questions.q: If a pigeon lives on our balcony, is the balcony part of the pigeon's home or ours?
big_questions.hint: Think about who uses the balcony, for what, and at what time of day.

big_questions.q: Is a city natural or made by people?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a city is built from, and about the trees, crows and microbes living in it.

big_questions.q: If there is no 'away', what should we do with things we no longer need?
big_questions.hint: Think of things that can rot, things that can be used again, and things that can be made into something new.

big_questions.q: The moong seedlings in the closed box kept growing. Did they notice the lid?
big_questions.hint: Plants sense light, water, touch and gravity. Did the seedlings change the way they grew when they reached the lid?

big_questions.q: Which living things share your environment without you ever seeing them?
big_questions.hint: Think of microbes in the soil, in curd and on your skin, and of animals that come out at night.

story.title: The Bottle on Ammamma's Shelf
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: water in a closed bottle evaporates, condenses on the cool glass and runs back down, and kitchen water really does travel through drains to treatment plants, lakes, rivers or the sea.
text: In the summer holidays, Arjun came from Hyderabad to stay with his cousin Kavya in Madurai. Arjun was seven. Kavya was nine, and she knew every corner of their grandmother's flat.

On the first morning, Arjun found a big glass bottle on the shelf by the window. It was round like a pot, with a narrow neck and a cork pushed in tight. Inside was a little green world. A money plant curled along the bottom. Soft moss covered a few stones. A tiny fern stood in one corner.
"Who waters it?" Arjun asked.
"Nobody," said Ammamma, from the kitchen. "I closed that bottle eight years ago. I have not opened it since."

Arjun looked at the plants. They were green and fresh. One money plant leaf was new and still pale. "That's not possible," he said. "Plants need water. You must be watering it at night when nobody sees."
Ammamma laughed. "Ask Kavya to help you find out."
Kavya pulled a stool up to the shelf. "Look at the glass, Arjun. Not the plants. The glass."

Arjun pressed his nose close. The inside of the glass was covered with tiny drops, like the outside of a cold tumbler of water. Near the top, the drops were so small they made the glass misty. Lower down, some drops had joined into bigger ones. As he watched, one big drop slid down the glass and disappeared into the moss.
"Water," said Arjun. "But where did it come from? There's a cork."
"Let's watch it all day," said Kavya. "Then you tell me."

So they did. In the cool early morning, the glass was misty all over. Kavya touched the outside. "Feel. The glass is cooler than the air inside the bottle. Water vapour from the soil and the leaves turns back into drops on the cool glass. That's called condensing."

By the afternoon, the sun had warmed the room. The mist on the glass was almost gone. Kavya pointed at the soil. "The drops ran down into the soil this morning. Now the warm soil and the leaves are giving the water back to the air inside. That's called evaporating. You can't see water vapour, but it's in there."
"So the same water goes up and down," said Arjun slowly. "Up from the soil and the leaves. Onto the glass. Down into the soil again."
"Every day," said Ammamma, "for eight years."
"What about air?" asked Arjun. "The plants need air too."

"In the light, the leaves make their food from water and a gas in the air called carbon dioxide," said Kavya. "They give out oxygen. Then the plants, and the tiny microbes in the soil, breathe some of that oxygen and give out carbon dioxide again. So the air goes round too."
Arjun sat back on the stool. He was quiet for a while. Then he said, "Nothing new goes in. Nothing goes out. Only the light."
That evening, after dinner, Arjun scraped the leftover rasam from his plate into the sink. He turned on the tap and washed it down. "There," he said. "Gone."
Kavya looked at him. "Gone where?"
Arjun opened his mouth and shut it again.

"Come," said Kavya. She took a torch, and they went out to the balcony. A grey pipe ran from under the kitchen sink, through the wall, and down the side of the building. They followed it with the torch, down past the flat below, and the one below that, to the ground. There it joined a bigger pipe that went under the road.
"Where does that one go?" Arjun asked.

Ammamma had come out behind them. "To a big drain, and then to a plant where the dirty water is cleaned," she said. "Then the cleaner water goes into a river or out to the sea. Not every city cleans all its drain water. In some places, it flows straight into a lake."
"So the rasam isn't gone," said Arjun. "It's just somewhere else."
"The water in it will rise from the sea one day as water vapour," said Kavya. "Then it will come down as rain. Maybe on Madurai."
Arjun looked up at the sky. The first stars were coming out above the temple towers. "Is the whole world like Ammamma's bottle?"

"In one way, yes," said Ammamma. "There is no glass around the Earth. But the Earth's pull holds the air and the water close. The sunlight comes in. The same water and the same air go round and round. Whatever we pour out or throw out stays in the bottle with us."
The next morning, Arjun was up before Kavya. She found him at the shelf, watching a drop slide down the glass. Beside him, on the floor, was a small steel bowl.
"What's that for?" Kavya asked.
"For the rice water," said Arjun. "Ammamma says it's good for her tulsi. I'm not washing it away any more. I'm sending it somewhere on purpose."
story.epiphany: For the parent: a closed bottle garden keeps going because water evaporates from the soil and leaves, condenses on the cooler glass and runs back down, and because plants and soil microbes keep passing oxygen and carbon dioxide between them. Only light enters. Earth works the same way for water and air: sunlight comes in and heat leaves, but almost no matter arrives or escapes. Arjun's leap is that 'washing it away' only moves the rasam somewhere else in that shared bottle.
ask: Where did the drops on the inside of Ammamma's bottle come from?
Why was the glass misty in the morning but clear in the afternoon?
What happened to Arjun's rasam after it went down the sink?
In what way is the Earth like Ammamma's bottle? In what way is it different?
What did Arjun decide to do with the rice water, and why?

games.title: Four Corners: living or not, natural or made
games.context: This is a card game about sorting the things around us. Each card shows one thing. Players place it in one of four corners of a grid, and must give a reason.

printables.title: 32 thing cards to cut out
items: Easy cards: crow, neem tree, stone, rain cloud, steel tumbler, plastic bucket, ant, sand, auto-rickshaw, coconut, river, brick
Tricky cards: curd, wooden spoon, potted tulsi, dry moong seed, cotton shirt, temple tank with fish, paper, salt from the salt pans, a dog, a mango tree your grandfather planted
More tricky cards: honey, a pearl, a silk saree, glass, a road with grass growing through cracks, a bird's nest, a beehive, a snake skin, a candle, a clay pot

printables.title: The four-corner grid
items: A big square split into four boxes: Living and natural, Living and placed or cared for by people, Non-living and natural, Non-living and made by people
A small 'Argue it!' circle in the middle, for cards that could go in two boxes

printables.title: Reason tokens
items: 20 small paper circles. A player earns one for every good reason that the others accept.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns to turn over one card.
Put the card in one of the four boxes, and say why in one sentence.
If another player thinks it belongs somewhere else, put it in the 'Argue it!' circle. Each of you gives a reason.
If the others agree with a reason, that player earns a reason token. A good reason can earn a token even if you change your mind.
When all cards are placed, the player with the most reason tokens wins.
Playing alone? Sort all the cards, then pick the three hardest and write a reason for each.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and lay out the grid. 2. Read the four box names aloud. 3. Place one easy card together, such as the crow.
flow.say: Each card is something in our environment. We put it in a box and say why. Let's try the crow together. Is the crow living? Is the crow natural?
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Is the thing living? Is it natural? Put it in a box.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Corners, a card game about sorting the things around us.

flow.do: Take turns turning over cards. When a card is argued, both players give a reason before you decide.
flow.say: Curd! Is curd living? Who made it? Tell me your reason before you put it down.
flow.kid: Say your reason out loud. Others can argue. Good reasons win tokens.
flow.parent: Expect real arguments over curd (made by people, but full of living bacteria), the wooden spoon (made by people from a natural, once-living tree), honey and the beehive (made by bees, not people) and the dry seed (alive though still). These are the point of the game. Reward the reason, not the box.

check.q: Which box suits a dry moong seed best?
check.why: A dry moong seed is alive, though they seem to do nothing. Given water, they sprout. Many people first say 'non-living', because the seed does not move or grow while dry.

flow.do: 1. Count the tokens. 2. Look at the 'Argue it!' cards together. 3. Ask which card was hardest.
flow.say: Which card was hardest to place? Why? Did anything belong to two boxes at once?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why was it hard?

ask.q: Why is a beehive hard to place?
good: It is made, but by bees, not by people.
It is natural, though it is built.
The box names only talk about people making things.

items: 4 blue water-drop tokens, one per player

rules: Each player puts a water drop on Home tap.
Take turns to roll a dice and move round the loop.
On a Choice square, take a choice card and do what it says. Tokens put on the board stay there.
If you land on a square with an oil or wrapper token, you are stuck there for one turn. Your drop is dirty and must be cleaned at the Treatment plant before it can go on.
A player can spend a turn to pick up one token and take it to the Dump yard. The dump yard is still part of the board.
The first drop to go all the way round twice wins. But if more than 10 tokens are on the board, everyone loses.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the board. 2. Put the drops on Home tap. 3. Read the squares round the loop aloud.
flow.say: This board is one loop. Our water starts at the tap and goes to the sink, the drain, the river, the cloud and the rain. Then it comes back to the tap.
flow.kid: Put your drop on Home tap. Follow the loop with your finger.
flow.context: This is the first step of No Away, a board game where everything you throw out stays on the board.

flow.do: Play. When someone places a token, ask where that thing would really go.
flow.say: You poured oil down the sink. Look, the oil stays on the Drain square. Who will land there next?
flow.kid: Roll and move. Read your card. Tokens stay on the board!
flow.parent: The point is that nothing leaves the loop. Even the Dump yard sits beside the board. If tokens pile up, everyone loses, so players soon start cleaning up together. Let that happen without telling them to.

flow.do: Count the tokens left on the board. Talk about which choice cards put the most on it.
flow.say: How many tokens are still on the board? Which choices put them there? Where would they be in real life?
flow.kid: Count the tokens left. Which cards made the most mess?

check.q: In the game, what happens to a wrapper token put on the River square?
options: It stays on the board until someone moves it
It turns into a water drop
check.why: Nothing leaves the board, just as nothing thrown away leaves the Earth. Even the Dump yard is beside the board. Choosing 'it leaves the board' is the 'away' habit the game is testing.

experiments.title: The Closed Box Test: can moong seedlings live with the lid on?
experiments.context: In this experiment you grow moong seeds in two clear boxes. One box is closed tight. The other is left open. You add no more water for a week, and watch what happens to the water and the seedlings in each.
experiments.question: If we shut moong seeds in a closed box with damp cotton, and add no more water or air, will they live longer or shorter than seeds in an open box?
experiments.predict: Which box will keep its seedlings green longer, the closed one or the open one? Why do you think so? Think about water, and think about air.
experiments.fair_test: Both boxes are the same size. Each gets the same cotton, the same 3 tablespoons of water and 10 soaked moong seeds from the same bowl. Both stand side by side in the same place. Only one thing is different: one box has its lid on. We use 10 seeds, not 1, because one seed might be dead.
results_table: Closed box: drops on the lid?
Closed box: cotton damp or dry?
Open box: cotton damp or dry?

materials.item: two clear plastic boxes of the same size with lids, such as takeaway food boxes. Two glass jars with lids also work, but the open jar dries more slowly, so the test takes longer.
cotton wool, enough for a layer about 1 cm thick in each box. No cotton? Use a folded cotton hanky or soil from a potted plant.
whole green moong seeds, soaked in water overnight
a tablespoon and water
a pen and two paper labels: 'Lid on' and 'Lid off'
a kitchen weighing scale, if you have one (not needed)

experiments.safety: Wash hands after handling the seeds and cotton. If white or grey fuzzy mould grows, do not open the box near your face. Throw the cotton and seeds in the wet waste at the end, and wash the boxes.

schedule.what: The night before: soak 20 moong seeds in a bowl of water.
Set up both boxes. Guess what will happen and why. Close one lid. Weigh both boxes if you have a scale.
Look for drops on the lid of the closed box. Touch the cotton in the open box. Fill in the table.
Look at both boxes again and fill in the table.
Last look and weighing. Say your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 2, 4 and 7. On day 7, draw both boxes side by side and draw arrows where you think the water went in each.

flow.do: The night before, put 20 whole moong seeds in a bowl and cover them with water.
flow.say: Tonight we soak some moong seeds, so they are ready to sprout tomorrow.
flow.kid: Put 20 moong seeds in a bowl. Cover them with water.
flow.parent: Soaking for 8 to 12 hours makes the seeds sprout within a day. Any whole green moong from the kitchen works. Split moong dal will not sprout.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Closed Box Test. You soak moong seeds the night before.

flow.do: 1. Lay cotton wool about 1 cm thick in each box. 2. Pour 3 tablespoons of water evenly over each cotton. 3. Spread 10 soaked seeds on each. 4. Label one box 'Lid on' and one 'Lid off'.
flow.say: Both boxes get exactly the same cotton, the same water and the same number of seeds. Why do you think that matters?
flow.kid: Put cotton in both boxes. Add 3 spoons of water to each. Put 10 seeds on each.
flow.parent: Count the spoons aloud together. Keeping everything the same means any difference must come from the lid. The cotton should be damp all through, with no pool of water on top.
flow.context: This is the setting-up step of the Closed Box Test.

flow.do: Hold up the lid. Ask your child to guess before you close it. Wait for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: I'm going to close this box tight and leave the other one open. We won't add any more water for a week. Which seeds do you think will do better? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which box will keep its seedlings green? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen in the closed box?
good: Any guess with a reason. Many children say the closed seeds will die because they have no air. Others say the closed box will keep its water. Both are good guesses.

flow.parent: Do not hint. Write the guess and the reason on the label or in the notebook, so you can look back on day 7.

flow.do: 1. Press the lid on one box firmly all round. 2. Put both boxes side by side in a bright place, out of direct sun. 3. If you have a kitchen scale, weigh each box and write the weights down.
flow.say: Now the closed box has nothing coming in except light. Let's put them where it is bright, but not in hot sun.
flow.kid: Close one lid tight. Put both boxes in a bright spot. No hot sun!
flow.parent: Direct sun can heat a closed box enough to cook the seedlings, so choose a bright windowsill that gets no midday sun, or a table near a window. A sunny balcony is too hot.

flow.do: Next morning: look closely at the lid of the closed box. Touch the cotton in the open box with one finger. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Look at the lid of the closed box. What do you see on it? Now feel the cotton in the open box. Is it as wet as yesterday?
flow.kid: Look at the closed lid. Drops? Feel the open box cotton. Still wet?
flow.parent: By morning, the inside of the closed lid is usually misty or covered with drops. Most seeds in both boxes have small white roots. Do not open the closed box at any point.

flow.do: On day 4: look at both boxes and fill in the table again.
flow.say: What has changed in each box since day 2? Look at the cotton, the drops and the seedlings.
flow.kid: Look at both boxes. What changed? Fill in your table.
flow.parent: In a warm Indian home, the open box's cotton is often dry by day 3 or 4, and those seedlings start to droop. In cool or rainy weather it may take a few days longer, so keep checking until there is a clear difference. The closed box should still be misty, with seedlings growing up towards the lid.

flow.do: On day 7: 1. Look at both boxes. 2. Weigh them again, if you weighed them on day 1. 3. Ask for a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What happened in each box? What did you see that tells you so? Why do you think it happened? If we weighed them, what happened to each weight?
flow.kid: What happened? What did you see? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Where did the water in the open box go?
good: Into the air of the room.
It evaporated.
Some went into the seedlings and out of their leaves into the room.

ask.q: Where did the water in the closed box go?
good: It went into the air in the box, onto the lid, and dripped back down.
It went round and round inside the box.
Nowhere outside the box.

flow.parent: With a scale, the closed box weighs almost the same as on day 1, within a few grams, even though the seedlings grew. Almost nothing left it. A takeaway lid is not perfectly airtight, so a tiny loss is normal. The open box is lighter, because water left it as vapour. If your closed box grew mould, that is another living thing that lived on the same water and air.

flow.do: Talk about why the closed seedlings did not run out of air. Then talk about Earth.
flow.say: The closed box never got new air. In the light, the leaves make oxygen, and the seedlings and microbes breathe it again. Earth is a bit like this box. What comes in from outside?
flow.kid: Nothing new came into the closed box. Only light. Is Earth like that?

check.q: What came into the closed box from outside during the week?
check.why: The lid kept water and air in and kept new water and air out. Only light came through the clear plastic. Picking 'fresh air' is a common guess, because we feel plants must need new air. The seedlings used the same air again and again.

experiments.title: The Drain Test: does washing powder in water change how seeds sprout?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sprout moong seeds with plain water, a little washing powder in water, and a lot of washing powder in water. Soapy water from our homes goes down drains and reaches lakes and rivers, where seeds and plants live.
experiments.question: Do moong seeds sprout and grow the same in soapy water as in plain water? Does the amount of soap matter?
experiments.predict: Which cup of seeds will grow the longest roots by day 3: plain water, a little soap or a lot of soap? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each cup gets the same cotton, 10 seeds from the same packet and 2 tablespoons of its own water. All three cups stand together in the same place. Only the water changes. We keep adding the same water to each cup if it dries.

materials.item: three small cups or steel katoris of the same size
cotton wool or a folded cotton cloth for each cup
30 whole green moong seeds, not soaked
washing powder, the kind used for clothes
three tumblers of water, labelled 'Plain', 'A little' and 'A lot'
a teaspoon, a tablespoon and a ruler

experiments.safety: A grown-up mixes the washing powder. Keep it away from eyes and mouths. Wash hands after touching soapy cotton. Pour the soapy water away at the end into the toilet, not onto a potted plant.

schedule.what: Mix the three waters. Set up three cups with 10 seeds each. Guess and give a reason.
Count the sprouted seeds in each cup. Add a spoon of the right water to any cup that is drying.
Count again and measure the longest root in each cup. Say your claim, evidence and reasoning.
One last look. Clear up.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 2 and 3. Draw one seedling from each cup, the same size as in real life.

flow.do: 1. Fill three tumblers with water. 2. Leave the first plain. 3. Stir a small pinch of washing powder into the second. 4. Stir 1 level teaspoon into the third. 5. Label them.
flow.say: Water from our washing goes down the drain. Some of it reaches lakes, where seeds and plants live. Let's see what soapy water does to seeds.
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes the soap. One plain, one a little, one a lot.
flow.parent: A pinch is about what you hold between two fingers. A level teaspoon in a tumbler is far stronger than most drain water, so it makes the effect easy to see.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Drain Test, which compares seeds in plain water and soapy water.

flow.do: 1. Put cotton in each cup. 2. Pour 2 tablespoons of the matching water on each. 3. Put 10 dry moong seeds on each cup. 4. Label the cups.
flow.say: Which cup do you think will grow the longest roots? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put 10 seeds on each cup. Guess which grows best. Why?

ask.q: What do you think the soap will do?
good: Any guess with a reason, for example that soap cleans, so it cannot hurt, or that soap is not meant for plants, so it may harm them.

flow.do: Put the three cups side by side in the same place, out of direct sun.
flow.say: All three cups sit together, so they get the same warmth and light. Only the water is different.
flow.kid: Put the three cups together. Wait till tomorrow.
flow.parent: If the cups dry out on day 2, add one more spoon of each cup's own water.

flow.do: Day 2: count how many seeds in each cup have a white root. Fill in the table.
flow.say: How many seeds have sprouted in each cup? Let's count them together.
flow.kid: Count the seeds with roots in each cup.

flow.do: Day 3: 1. Count again. 2. Measure the longest root in each cup with a ruler. 3. Ask for a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What did the soap do? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: What did the soap do? Show me how you know.
flow.parent: Usually the plain cup grows the longest white roots. The 'a lot' cup has fewer sprouts, or short, brownish roots. The 'a little' cup is often in between, or close to plain. If all three grow the same in your home, that is a real result too. Write it down, and talk about how much soap a lake would need to get.

activities.title: The Window Survey: what is in our environment?
activities.context: This activity starts the unit. You list everything you can see, hear and feel from one window, then sort the list into living and non-living, and natural and made by people.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a timer or a phone clock

activities.safety: Stay inside the window or the balcony railing. Do not lean out.

schedule.what: List what you notice from one window in 3 minutes, then sort the list.

activities.record: Draw a big square split into four boxes: living and natural, living and cared for by people, non-living and natural, non-living and made by people. Write each thing from your list in a box.

flow.do: 1. Stand at a window or balcony together. 2. Set a 3-minute timer. 3. Your child calls out everything they see, hear or feel. 4. You write it all down.
flow.say: For three minutes, tell me everything you notice. Things you see, things you hear, things you feel on your skin. I'll write them all down.
flow.kid: Look, listen and feel for 3 minutes. Say everything you notice.
flow.parent: Children often list only big things they see. Prompt gently: 'What can you hear? What can you feel on your face?' Good lists include wind, sunlight, a crow, a coconut palm, an auto, a temple bell, a neighbour's pressure cooker, dust, clouds and the smell of jasmine.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Window Survey, which starts the unit on our environment.

flow.do: 1. Draw the four-box square. 2. Read out each thing on the list. 3. Your child says which box it goes in, and why.
flow.say: Everything on our list is part of our environment. Let's sort it. Is the crow living or non-living? Natural or made by people?
flow.kid: Sort your list into the four boxes. Say why for each.

good: Non-living and natural.

ask.q: Where does the potted plant on the next balcony go?
good: Living, and cared for by people.
Living and natural, but someone planted them.

flow.do: Look at the box with the most things, and the things that were hard to place.
flow.say: Which box has the most things? Which thing was hardest to place? Did anything change something else on the list?
flow.kid: Which box is fullest? Which thing was hard? Why?

ask.q: Can you find one thing on the list that changes another thing on the list?
good: The sun warms the wall.
The wind moves the tree.
The crow eats from the dustbin.
The auto makes smoke in the air.

check.q: Lakshmi hears a temple bell from her window. Which box does the bell go in?
check.why: A bell is made of metal by people, and it is not alive. The sound reaches Lakshmi through the air. Picking 'natural' happens when we think of the sound, which travels through the natural air, instead of the bell that makes it.

setup.caption: 1. Three minutes: say everything you see, hear and feel.

setup.art: A notebook page with a square split into four labelled boxes, and words like crow, wind, auto, palm, bell written in them.

activities.title: Where Is Away? Follow the water and the rubbish
activities.context: In this activity you follow your kitchen water and your rubbish as far as you can, to find out where 'away' really is.

materials.item: a torch
a notebook and pencil
a sheet of paper for a map

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along. Stay away from open drains, roads and moving vehicles. Do not touch the drain or the bins.

schedule.what: Follow the sink pipe as far as you can see it. Ask who takes the rubbish and where. Draw a map of where both go.

activities.record: Draw a map with two paths: one for the sink water and one for the dry rubbish. Draw each path as far as you know it. Put a question mark where you do not know.

flow.do: 1. Look under the kitchen sink together. 2. Find where the pipe leaves the flat. 3. From a balcony or the ground, follow it with your eyes or a torch as far as you can.
flow.say: When water goes down the sink, we say it has gone away. Let's find out where away is. Where does this pipe go?
flow.kid: Find the sink pipe. Where does it go? Follow it with your eyes.
flow.parent: In most flats, the pipe runs down the outside of the building into a bigger pipe or an inspection chamber, and then into the street sewer. You do not need to see all of it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Is Away?, an activity that follows our kitchen water and rubbish.

flow.do: Ask the person who collects your rubbish, the building watchman, or a neighbour where the rubbish goes. Or look it up together on your city corporation's website.
flow.say: Who takes our rubbish? Where do they take it? Let's ask.
flow.kid: Who takes our rubbish? Ask where it goes next.
flow.parent: In many cities, rubbish goes first to a collection point or transfer station, then to a dump yard or a processing plant. In Chennai, the large dump yards are at Kodungaiyur and Perungudi. Wet waste may go to a compost centre, if it was kept separate.

flow.do: Draw the map of both paths together. Mark what you know and what you do not.
flow.say: Let's draw where our water and our rubbish go. Where does each path stop? Is that really the end?
flow.kid: Draw the paths. Does either one really end?

ask.q: Where does the sink water end up in the end?
good: A river, a lake or the sea.
Then it evaporates and becomes rain again.
It never really ends.

check.q: Farhan washes a plastic wrapper down a street drain. Where is the wrapper most likely to end up?
options: In a river, a lake or the sea, or stuck in the drain
It turns into soil within a week
check.why: Plastic does not rot away within weeks, and it does not disappear. Drains carry it to rivers, lakes and the sea, or it blocks the drain. 'It disappears' is the 'away' habit: thinking that what we cannot see any more has stopped existing.

activities.title: Who Else Lives Here? A week of home neighbours
activities.context: In this activity you find the other living things that share your flat or building, and notice what each one needs from the place where you find them.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a torch
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: Look, do not touch. Keep away from wasps' nests, bees and stray dogs. Wash hands after looking in corners.

schedule.what: Hunt through the flat for other living things. Write where you found each one.
Look again at one spot, morning or night.
Count up your list. For each living thing, say what the spot gives them.

activities.record: Make a table with three columns: who I found, where I found them, and what that spot gives them.

flow.do: Walk through the flat together. Look in the kitchen, the bathroom and the balcony. Check the window grills, the corners near the tube light and the potted plants.
flow.say: We are not the only ones living here. Let's find who else shares our home. Look in corners, near the light and near food.
flow.kid: Hunt for living things in your home. Write where each one was.
flow.parent: Common finds: ants near the sugar or the dustbin, a gecko near the tube light at night, a spider in a corner, pigeons or sparrows on the grill, mosquitoes in the bathroom, moss or black mould in a damp corner, and the potted plants. Mould and moss count as living things too.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Else Lives Here?, an activity about the living things that share our home.

flow.do: On another day, look again at one spot at a different time of day, such as the tube light after dark.
flow.say: Is the same living thing there now? Is someone new here?
flow.kid: Look at one spot again, at a new time. Who is there now?
flow.parent: A gecko waits near a tube light after dark because insects come to the light. Seeing this links the non-living part, the light, with the living ones.

flow.do: Count up the list. For each living thing, talk about what that spot gives them.
flow.say: Why do you think the ants are near the sugar jar, and the moss is in the damp corner? What does each spot give them?
flow.kid: Why is each one in that spot? What does the spot give them?

ask.q: Why is moss found in the damp corner of the bathroom and not on the sunny wall?
good: Moss needs damp places.
The sunny wall is too dry for moss.
The water in the bathroom keeps the corner wet.

activities.title: Natural, Made or Both? The kitchen hunt
activities.context: In this activity you find things in the kitchen and trace each one back to what it was made from, to find out how much of 'made by people' started as natural.

materials.item: 10 things from the kitchen, such as a steel tumbler, a wooden spoon, a clay pot, a bowl of curd, salt, rice, a plastic box, a glass jar, a cotton cloth and honey
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Leave knives, the stove and the gas cylinder alone.

schedule.what: Collect 10 kitchen things. For each one, say whether it is natural, made by people or both, and what it came from.

activities.record: Write each thing in a row, and draw an arrow back to what it was made from. For example: steel tumbler, from steel, from iron ore dug from the ground.

flow.do: Collect 10 things from the kitchen and put them on the floor or a table.
flow.say: Let's collect ten things from the kitchen. Then we decide: natural, made by people, or both?
flow.kid: Find 10 things in the kitchen. Put them in a row.
flow.context: This is the first step of the kitchen hunt, an activity about natural things and things made by people.

flow.do: For each thing, ask: natural, made by people, or both? Then ask: what was it made from, and what was that made from?
flow.say: This steel tumbler was made by people. What is steel made from? Where did that come from? Keep going back.
flow.kid: For each thing, ask: what was it made from? Keep asking!
flow.parent: Every made thing leads back to something natural: steel from iron ore, plastic mostly from oil or natural gas, glass from sand, paper from wood, a cotton cloth from the cotton plant, a clay pot from clay. Curd and honey are both: made with the help of living things. This prepares for the idea that what we make and throw out stays in the environment.

check.q: Divya's plastic lunch box is made by people. What was the plastic mostly made from?
options: Oil or natural gas from under the ground
check.why: Most plastic is made from oil or natural gas dug from under the ground. People change natural materials into new ones. They never make a material from nothing. Glass is the thing made from sand.

activities.title: One Tree's Guests (if you have a park or a tree nearby)
activities.context: In this activity you watch one tree for 15 minutes and list every living thing that uses the tree. It works on a street tree, a park tree or a tree seen from a balcony.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a cloth to sit on

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along. Do not touch ants' nests, bees' nests or caterpillars, because some sting or have itchy hairs. Stay away from the road.

schedule.what: Watch one tree for 15 minutes. List every living thing on it, under it and visiting it.

activities.record: Draw the tree. Draw each guest where you saw them, and write what they were doing.

flow.do: Choose one tree. Sit quietly where you can see it. For 15 minutes, list every living thing on it, under it, or visiting it.
flow.say: A tree is part of the environment of many others. Let's count who uses this one. Watch the trunk, the leaves, the ground under it and the sky above.
flow.kid: Watch one tree quietly. List every living thing you see.
flow.parent: On a neem, peepal, mango or rain tree you may see crows, mynas, squirrels, ants on the trunk, spiders, caterpillars, moss or lichen on the bark, and people resting in the shade. Saalumarada Thimmakka of Karnataka, with her husband, planted and cared for 385 banyan trees along about 4 km of road between Hulikal and Kudur. You could tell this story while you watch.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Tree's Guests, an activity for families with a tree nearby.

flow.do: Look at the list together.
flow.say: How many living things use this one tree? What does the tree give each of them? What do they give the tree?
flow.kid: How many guests did the tree have? What did the tree give them?

ask.q: What does a tree give a crow?
good: A place to sit or nest.
Shade.
Fruit or insects to eat.
