projects.title: A Bottle Garden to Keep
projects.context: In this month-long project you build a closed bottle garden with soil and a money plant cutting, close the jar, and keep a diary of the water going round inside.

materials.item: a big clear jar or bottle with a lid or cork, at least 1 litre, such as a large pickle jar
a cup of small stones or broken bits of clay pot
2 cups of soil from a potted plant, or potting soil
a small cutting of money plant with 3 or 4 leaves, or a small fern
a spoon and a long stick for pressing the soil

projects.safety: A grown-up handles the glass jar. Wash hands after handling soil. Keep the jar out of direct sun, or it gets too hot inside.

schedule.what: Build the bottle garden, water it once and close it.
Diary: drops on the glass in the morning and the afternoon.
Diary: new leaves or roots? Draw the garden.
Diary: anything new growing that you did not plant?
Diary: compare with day 1. Decide whether to keep it closed.

projects.record: A garden diary: the date, the time, what the glass looks like, and a drawing each week.

flow.do: 1. Put 2 cm of small stones in the bottom of the jar. 2. Add soil on top, about 5 cm deep. 3. Make a hole with the stick and plant the cutting. 4. Pour in 3 tablespoons of water. 5. Close the lid.
flow.say: We are making a little world. Stones at the bottom catch extra water. The soil holds the plant. After today, we will not open it.
flow.kid: Stones first, then soil. Plant the cutting. Water once. Close the lid.
flow.parent: If thick drops cover the glass all day after the first few days, there is too much water: open it for an afternoon, then close it again. If no drops form at all, add one more tablespoon of water. Small mould spots at first are common and usually fade.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Bottle Garden project, where you build a closed world in a jar.

flow.do: Look at the glass in the early morning and again in the afternoon. Write and draw what you see.
flow.say: When is the glass misty, morning or afternoon? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Is the glass misty now? Write the time and what you see.
flow.parent: Morning mist and afternoon clearing is common, because the glass is cooler than the air inside in the early morning.

flow.do: Every week, draw the garden and look for changes: new leaves, roots, moss, tiny insects or mould.
flow.say: Is anything living in there that we did not put in?
flow.kid: Draw your garden. Is anything new living there?
flow.parent: Tiny springtails, moss or a sprouted weed seed from the soil may appear. They came in with the soil. This shows the soil was full of life to begin with.

flow.do: Compare the day 1 drawing with today's. Talk about where the water has been all month.
flow.say: No water has gone in for a month. Where has the plant's water been all this time?
flow.kid: Look at day 1 and today. Where did the water go all month?

setup.art: A big glass pickle jar on newspaper, with a layer of small stones at the bottom and a child's hands spooning soil on top.
setup.caption: 1. Stones, then soil, then the cutting.

setup.art: The closed jar on a shelf near a window, with a money plant cutting inside and mist on the glass.
setup.caption: 2. Water once, close it, and keep a diary.

projects.title: Our Family's Care Week
projects.context: In this week-long project your family chooses one thing it sends out of the home, tries to send less of it for a week, and measures whether it worked.

materials.item: a notebook for a tally chart
whatever your chosen change needs, such as a cloth bag, a steel bowl for rice water or a small compost pot

projects.safety: If you choose composting, keep the pot covered and away from the kitchen counter. Wash hands after handling waste.

schedule.what: Choose one thing to send out less of. Count how much goes out on a normal day.
Start the change. Tally each day.
Count up the week. Did it work? What was hard? Will you keep it up?

projects.record: A tally chart with one row for each day: how many plastic bags, or how many litres of water, or how many bowls of peels kept out of the bin.

flow.do: Talk as a family. Choose one thing, such as plastic bags, oil down the sink, or peels in the dry bin. Count how much goes out on one normal day.
flow.say: We send many things out of our home. Let's pick one and try to send less of it this week. First, how much goes out on a normal day?
flow.kid: Pick one thing your family throws out. Count it for one day.
flow.parent: Good choices are small and countable: plastic carry bags brought home, leftover cooking oil, rice water poured down the sink, or wet waste mixed with dry. A change the child can do themselves works best.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Care Week project, where your family tries one change for a week.

flow.do: Each day, make the change and add a tally mark.
flow.say: Did we do it today? Let's add today's tally.
flow.kid: Did we do it today? Add a tally mark.

flow.do: At the end of the week, count up and compare with the first day.
flow.say: How much less went out this week? What made it hard? Where would the things we did not throw out have gone?
flow.kid: Count up. Did it work? What was hard?

ask.q: Should we keep doing it? Why?
good: Any answer with a reason, such as that it was easy, it saved money, or that a different change would be easier.

setup.art: A family at a dining table with a notebook, deciding between a cloth bag, a steel bowl and a small compost pot.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one change and count a normal day.

setup.art: A tally chart on the fridge with seven rows of marks, and a cloth bag hanging on a hook beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Tally every day, then count up the week.

challenges.title: A Water Bowl for Birds on a Hot Balcony
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In an Indian summer, birds in cities struggle to find water. Design a water station for your balcony or window that birds will use safely.
challenges.problem: Make a water station for birds that stays cool, is easy to clean every day, keeps birds safe from cats and does not become a place for mosquitoes to breed.
constraints: Use things from home, such as a clay saucer, a steel plate, stones and string.
It must be fixed so it cannot fall off the balcony.
The water must be easy to change every day.
materials: a wide, shallow clay saucer or steel plate
a piece of cloth or cardboard for shade
general: A wide, shallow dish is best, about 3 to 5 cm deep, so small birds can stand and drink without falling in.
Clay keeps water cooler than plastic, because water seeps into the clay and evaporates from the outside.
Change the water every day, so mosquito eggs never have time to hatch.
creative: Put a stone in the middle as a landing step.
Hang a small cloth over one side for shade.
Keep a second saucer for washing and swapping, so one is always clean.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own bird water station. Draw it, build it with a grown-up, and keep a tally of the birds that visit for one week.

flow.do: Talk about the problem. Draw two ideas.
flow.say: Birds need water in summer, but a bowl can fall, get hot, or grow mosquitoes. What could we build? Let's each draw one idea.
flow.kid: Draw two ideas for a bird water bowl. Think: safe, cool, clean.
flow.context: This is a design challenge: make a water station for birds on a hot balcony.

flow.do: Build the best idea. Fix it firmly where a grown-up says.
flow.say: Where can we put it so cats cannot reach it and it will not fall?
flow.kid: Build it with a grown-up. Fix it so it cannot fall.
flow.parent: Fix the dish on the inside of the railing or on a wide ledge, never hanging over the edge. A ledge out of reach of cats is best.

flow.do: Make a plan for changing the water every day.
flow.say: Who will change the water each morning? Why does it matter to change it every day?
flow.kid: Who changes the water each day? Why every day?

check.q: Why should the water in a bird bowl be changed every day?
options: So mosquito eggs in it never have time to hatch into mosquitoes
Because birds only drink fresh water once
check.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, and the young take several days to grow into flying mosquitoes. Changing the water every day tips them out first. Some mosquitoes spread dengue, so this matters for people too.

setup.art: A shallow clay saucer with a stone in the middle, tied firmly on a wide balcony ledge, with a cloth giving shade on one side.
setup.caption: 1. Design a cool, safe, shallow water bowl.

setup.art: A myna drinking from the saucer while a child watches from inside and makes a tally mark.
setup.caption: 2. Change the water every day and count the visitors.

challenges.title: Stop It at the Sink: a catcher for food bits and oil
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Food bits and cooking oil washed down the kitchen sink can block pipes and dirty the water downstream. Design a way to catch them before they go down.
challenges.problem: Design a way to stop rice, peels and oil going down the kitchen sink, using things from home, that the family will really use every day.
constraints: It must not block the sink.
It must be easy to empty into the wet waste bin.
It must be safe and cost nothing or very little.
materials: a steel tea strainer or a small sieve
old newspaper or a used cloth
a small steel bowl or tin with a lid
general: Put a steel mesh catcher over the sink hole and empty it into the wet waste.
Wipe oily pans and plates with old newspaper before washing, and put the paper in the dry waste.
Pour leftover oil into a tin with a lid, not the sink.
creative: Make a sign for the sink that reminds everyone.
Use the starchy rice water to water plants instead of pouring it out.
Keep a 'scrape plate' by the sink for leftovers.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way to stop it at the sink. Try it for three days and ask the family what worked.

flow.do: Look at what goes down the sink after one meal. Talk about where it goes.
flow.say: After lunch, let's watch what goes down the sink. Where does it go after that?
flow.kid: Watch the sink after lunch. What goes down? Where next?
flow.context: This is a design challenge: catch food bits and oil before they go down the sink.

flow.do: Draw and build a catcher. Try it after the next meal.
flow.say: What could catch the rice but let the water through? What could catch the oil?
flow.kid: Make a catcher. Try it after the next meal.
flow.parent: A steel tea strainer over the sink hole catches most bits. Oil needs to be wiped off before washing, because a strainer lets it through.

flow.do: Look at what the catcher caught.
flow.say: How much did we catch? Where will it go now instead?
flow.kid: What did your catcher catch? Where will it go now?

check.q: Why does a tea strainer not stop oil going down the sink?
options: Oil is a liquid, so it flows through the holes
Oil turns into water in the sink
check.why: Oil is a liquid, like water, so it runs through the mesh. Wiping the pan with paper first catches it. In the pipes, cooled oil and fat can stick and build up into a blockage.

setup.art: A steel kitchen sink with a tea strainer set over the drain hole, holding a few grains of rice and a peel.
setup.caption: 1. Catch the food bits over the drain.

setup.art: A child wiping an oily kadai with a sheet of old newspaper before washing it.
setup.caption: 2. Wipe the oil off first, before washing.

videos.title: A sealed bottle garden that has lived for decades
videos.why: Shows a real closed bottle garden with drops on the glass, like the Closed Box Test and the Bottle Garden project, on a bigger scale.
videos.check: No video id has been checked yet. Search for 'David Latimer bottle garden' or 'sealed terrarium water cycle'. Choose one that shows condensation on the glass and does not claim the plants need nothing at all: they still need light.

videos.title: Biosphere 2: what happened when eight people were sealed inside
videos.why: For the parent and older children: the true story in How We Found Out, with pictures of the glass building and its rainforest, ocean and farm.
videos.check: No video id has been checked yet. Prefer a short documentary clip or a Biosphere 2 (University of Arizona) video. Check that it explains the oxygen loss as soil microbes plus carbon dioxide taken up by concrete.

videos.title: Where does the water from our drains go? A sewage treatment plant in India
videos.why: Follows waste water from homes through a treatment plant, matching the Where Is Away? activity and the card on 'away'.
videos.check: No video id has been checked yet. Prefer a tour of an Indian city's plant, for example in Chennai or Bengaluru. Check that it shows screening, settling and cleaning by microbes, and is suitable for children.

opts: Only forests, rivers and wild animals
Everything around a living thing that affects them
Only the things people have built
quiz.why: The environment is everything around a living thing that affects them: air, water, soil, light, other living things and things people make. Picking 'only forests' is a common idea, but a city flat has an environment too.

quiz.p: Which of these is part of the living environment?
opts: The sunlight on the floor
The ants in the kitchen
The water in the tap
quiz.why: Ants are alive: they eat, breathe, grow and make young. Sunlight and tap water are important parts of the environment, but they are non-living, so they belong to the physical environment.

quiz.p: Meena, a girl in Class 3, has a wooden spoon. Which is true about the spoon?
opts: It is natural and living
It was made by people from wood, which came from a living tree
It was made by people from nothing
quiz.why: People made the spoon, but they made it from wood, and wood comes from a tree. The spoon itself is not alive. People always make things from natural materials, never from nothing.

quiz.p: Which of these is a bit of both natural and made by people?
opts: A cloud
A plastic bucket
A bowl of curd
quiz.why: People make curd by adding a spoon of old curd to warm milk, but living bacteria do the work of turning the milk into curd. A cloud is fully natural. A bucket is made by people.

quiz.p: In the Closed Box Test, drops formed on the inside of the closed lid. Where did the water in the drops come from?
opts: From the air outside the box
From the cotton and the seedlings inside the box
From the plastic of the lid
quiz.why: The lid kept outside air out. Water evaporated from the wet cotton and the seedlings' leaves, then condensed on the cooler lid. Picking 'from outside' is common, because we expect water to have been brought in.

quiz.p: In the Closed Box Test, the open box dried out. Why?
opts: Its water evaporated into the air of the room and did not come back
The seedlings drank all of it and kept it
The cotton turned it into air
quiz.why: The open box let water vapour escape into the room. In the closed box the same vapour hit the lid and dripped back. The seedlings did drink some, but they gave much of it to the air through their leaves.

quiz.p: How is Earth like the closed box?
opts: New water rains in from space every day
Sunlight comes in, but almost no new water or air arrives, so the same water and air go round
Nothing at all comes in, not even light
quiz.why: Sunlight reaches Earth from outside, and heat goes back out to space. But gravity holds the air and water close, and almost no new matter arrives. So water and air are used again and again.

quiz.p: Kavya pours leftover rasam down the sink. Where does the rasam go?
opts: It disappears
Through drains to a treatment plant, a river, a lake or the sea
Back into Kavya's tap
quiz.why: Nothing poured down a sink leaves the Earth. It travels through drains, and some is cleaned at treatment plants, before reaching rivers, lakes or the sea. 'It disappears' is the 'away' habit.

quiz.p: Moss grows in the damp corner of a bathroom but not on a hot, sunny wall. What does this show?
opts: The non-living environment decides where some living things can live
Moss is scared of light
Moss is non-living
quiz.why: Moss needs damp places, so the water and shade in the bathroom corner make it a home for moss. The dry sunny wall does not. The physical environment shapes who can live where.

quiz.p: Farhan's family wants to send less plastic out of their home. Which plan is easiest to check?
opts: Try to be better
Carry a cloth bag to the shop and count the plastic bags brought home each day for a week
Tell the neighbours to use less plastic
quiz.why: A good care plan is one change you can count. Counting the bags each day shows whether it worked. 'Try to be better' is a good wish, but there is nothing to count.

items.p: Sort these into the living environment or the physical (non-living) environment.
items.a: see items
items.why: Living things grow, breathe and make young. Everything else around us is the physical environment. A strong sorter asks 'Is it alive?' and not 'Does it move?', because wind moves but is not alive.

items.p: Sort these into natural or made by people.
items.a: see items
items.why: Natural things are made by nature. Made things are made by people from natural materials. A strong sorter can say what each made thing came from.

items.p: Everything around a living thing that affects them is called their ____.
items.why: The environment includes living and non-living things, natural and made.

items.p: Which of these is NOT part of a pigeon's environment on a city balcony?
opts: the railing they sit on
the grain someone scatters
a lion in a forest far away
items.why: A pigeon's environment is everything around them that affects them. A lion far away does not affect the pigeon. The railing and the grain do.

items.p: A city flat has no environment, because there are no forests in it.
items.why: False. A flat has air, water, light, warmth, ants, geckos, plants and people. All of that is an environment.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 3, says, "A dry moong seed is non-living, because they do not move or grow." Is she right? Explain.
items.a: No. A dry moong seed is alive, though they seem to do nothing. Given water, they swell and sprout within a day or two. A stone never does that.
items.why: A strong answer says the seed is alive and gives evidence, such as sprouting when given water.

items.p: In the Closed Box Test, what was the ONE thing that was different between the two boxes?
opts: the number of seeds
the lid
the amount of water
items.why: Everything else was kept the same: the box, the cotton, the water, the seeds and the place. That is why any difference must come from the lid.

items.p: Draw the closed box from the Closed Box Test. Draw arrows to show where the water went: from the cotton, into the air, onto the lid and back down.
items.art: A blank outline of a clear box with a lid, with cotton and three seedlings drawn at the bottom.
items.a: A box with cotton and seedlings, arrows going up from the cotton and the leaves, drops on the lid, and arrows going back down to the cotton.
items.why: A strong drawing makes the water go round in a loop, and shows that none leaves the box.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a liquid slowly turns into a gas in the air
water vapour cools and turns back into drops
the non-living part of the environment
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit.

items.p: Put these in the order your kitchen water travels after it leaves the sink.
items.why: Waste water flows down the pipe, into the street drain, and to a treatment plant, then on to a river or the sea. A strong answer also knows that the journey does not end there: the water rises again as vapour.

items.p: Give one example of a living thing changing the non-living environment.
items.a: For example: a peepal's roots crack a wall, a plant gives water to the air through their leaves, or earthworms turn dead leaves into soil.
items.why: A strong answer names the living thing, the non-living thing and what changes.

items.p: A gecko waits next to the tube light every night. Why there?
opts: The light warms the gecko like the Sun
Insects come to the light, so there is food there
Geckos like to look at bright things
items.why: Many insects fly to lights at night, so the light brings the gecko food. This is a non-living part of the environment, the light, shaping where a living thing spends their time.

items.p: Everything people make was made from something natural first.
items.why: True. Steel comes from iron ore, plastic mostly from oil or gas, glass from sand, paper from wood. People change natural materials. They never make one from nothing.

items.p: A family in Chennai is deciding what to do with the peels and leftover food from the kitchen.

views.says: Let's make compost on the balcony. Then the peels become soil for our plants instead of going to the dump yard.
Compost will smell and bring flies in a small flat. Let the corporation take it away.
Let's keep wet waste in its own bin, so the corporation can compost it at their centre.

items.ask: Which plan do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason from this unit, for example that peels in the dry bin go to the dump yard and rot there in a smelly heap, while a compost pot turns them into soil for the plants. It then says one thing another person has right, such as that composting in a small flat needs a covered pot and some care.
items.why: There is a real trade-off. Composting at home sends less to the dump, but it takes space and effort. Separate bins only help if the city collects them separately.

items.p: Draw your window. Draw and label two living things and two non-living things you can see from it.
items.a: A drawing of the window with four labelled things, two living (for example a crow and a tree) and two non-living (for example a road and the sun).
items.why: A strong drawing labels each thing and puts it in the right group.

items.p: In the Closed Box Test, the seedlings in the closed box never got fresh air. Explain how they still had the gases they needed.
items.a: In the light, their leaves made food from water and carbon dioxide and gave out oxygen. The seedlings and the microbes in the box breathed some of that oxygen and gave out carbon dioxide again. So the same air went round.
items.why: A strong answer names both gases and says they are used and given out again inside the box.

items.p: Priya weighs both boxes on day 1 and day 7 of the Closed Box Test. The seedlings in the closed box grew taller. What happens to the closed box's weight?
opts: It gets much heavier, because the seedlings grew
It stays about the same, because nothing went in or out
It gets much lighter, like the open box
items.why: Nothing went in or out of the closed box, so its weight stayed about the same, even though the seedlings grew. They were built from water and air that were already in the box. The open box got lighter, because water vapour left it.

items.p: The open box in the Closed Box Test got lighter because its water was destroyed.
items.why: False. The water was not destroyed. It evaporated into the room's air as water vapour. Later it may condense on a cold window or rise into a cloud.

items.p: Divya's family pours soapy water from washing clothes into the street drain. Use the Drain Test to explain what this water might do in a lake.
items.a: The Drain Test showed that a lot of washing powder in water made fewer seeds sprout, with shorter roots. If lots of soapy water reaches a lake, it may harm the seeds and plants that live there. In Bellandur Lake in Bengaluru, soap and sewage made thick froth.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence from the test and links it to living things in a lake.

items.p: In the Drain Test, why did each cup get 10 seeds and not just 1?
opts: Because 10 is a nice number
Because one seed might be dead, which would fool us
Because seeds need friends to sprout
items.why: One seed might be dead or damaged and fail to sprout for their own reason. With 10, one bad seed changes the count only a little, so the result is fairer.

items.p: Sort these: does each one mostly go round inside the Earth, or does it come from outside the Earth?
items.a: see items
items.why: Sunlight comes from the Sun, outside the Earth. Water, air, soil and the stuff in plastic stay on Earth and go round. A tiny amount of space dust also arrives each day.

items.p: When water vapour cools on a cold lid and turns into drops, we say it ____.
items.why: Condensing is the opposite of evaporating. Drops on the closed box lid formed this way.

items.p: Match each thing to where it most often goes in a city when we throw it out.
pairs: a drain, then a treatment plant or a river
a plastic wrapper in the dry bin
a dump yard or a recycling centre
peels kept in their own bin
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each thing goes somewhere in the environment. None of them leaves the Earth.

items.p: Arjun says, "It doesn't matter if I drop a wrapper. Someone will take it away." Use the idea of 'away' to answer him.
items.a: There is no away outside the Earth. If someone picks it up, it goes to a dump yard. If not, rain washes it into a drain, and it may reach a lake or the sea. Either way, it is still in the environment.
items.why: A strong answer says where the wrapper would really go.

items.p: Which of these changes the environment the MOST?
opts: one crow building a nest
people building a new city
an ant carrying a crumb
items.why: One crow or ant makes only small changes. People build cities, cut and plant forests, dig lakes and send out smoke and sewage, so people change the environment the most.

items.p: Draw a peepal growing out of a crack in an old wall. Draw how their roots change the wall over many years.
items.art: A blank outline of a brick wall with one small crack.
items.a: A wall with a crack, a peepal sapling, and roots pushing into the crack, making it wider, with a few bricks loose.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the living thing changing a non-living thing, slowly, by growing.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, for what happened in the closed box each day.
items: vapour condenses on the cooler lid
water evaporates from the cotton and leaves
drops run back down to the cotton
water vapour fills the air in the box
a: water evaporates from the cotton and leaves
water vapour fills the air in the box
vapour condenses on the cooler lid
drops run back down to the cotton
items.why: This is a loop, so after the last step the first one starts again. A strong answer says the same water keeps going round.

items.p: Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by living things.
items.why: True. Early Earth had almost no oxygen in its air. Tiny living things in the sea, and later plants and algae, made it in sunlight over billions of years.

items.p: A city is deciding what to do with a lake that has become dirty with sewage and rubbish.

views.who: Kavitha, a scientist who studies lakes
views.says: First stop the sewage flowing in. Build treatment plants. Otherwise the lake will just get dirty again.

views.who: Fatima, who lives next to the lake
views.says: Clear the rubbish now and plant trees round it. People will care for a lake they can enjoy.
Fill the lake in and build flats. The city needs homes.

items.ask: Which plan do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer back from one other side.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with a reason from this unit, for example that sewage must be stopped first or the lake will get dirty again, because what is poured out stays in the environment. It then says what another side has right.
items.why: These views all hold some truth. Cleaning without stopping new sewage does not last. Building on the lake removes a home for fish and birds and a place for rain to go.

items.p: The non-living part of the environment, such as air, water, soil and light, is called the ____ environment.
items.why: Books split the environment into the physical (non-living) and the biological (living) environment.

items.p: Biosphere 2 was a huge sealed glass building with plants, soil, animals and eight people inside. The oxygen slowly fell. Its soil had lots of compost, full of microbes. Explain why the oxygen might have fallen.
items.a: The microbes in the rich soil were breaking down the compost, and they breathe oxygen as they do it. They used up oxygen faster than the plants made it. So the oxygen in the sealed building slowly fell.
items.why: A strong answer says that microbes are living things that use oxygen, and that in a sealed place nothing new can come in to replace it.

items.p: In Biosphere 2, the microbes should also have made extra carbon dioxide. But the carbon dioxide did not rise as much as expected. Scientists found it was being taken up by something in the building. What was it?
opts: The glass windows
The bare concrete walls
The people's clothes
items.why: The bare, fresh concrete reacted with carbon dioxide and locked it away. The building itself was part of the environment inside, though nobody had planned it that way. This is why Jeff Severinghaus and others had to look so hard for the missing gas.

items.p: Explain why a closed box can keep its seedlings alive for a week without new water, but a city cannot keep its lakes clean without caring what goes into them. Use the idea that the same water goes round.
items.a: In the closed box, the same clean water goes round and is used again. In a city, the same water also goes round, but whatever we add to it, such as soap, oil and sewage, goes round with it into lakes and rivers. So keeping the water clean depends on what we put in.
items.why: A strong answer links the closed box and the city with the idea that water goes round, and adds that what we add goes round too.

items.p: Three people argue about whether a city flat is part of nature.

views.says: A flat is part of nature. Ants, geckos and moss live in it, and it is made of sand, stone and iron from the Earth.
A flat is made by people, so it is not nature. Nature is forests and rivers.
People are part of nature, so everything people make is part of nature too, like a bird's nest.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, with evidence from this unit. Then answer back from another view.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and backs it with evidence, such as the ants, geckos and moss found in the Who Else Lives Here? hunt, or that the flat is built from natural materials. It then answers back from another view.
items.why: This is a real disagreement about the word 'nature'. Each view is partly right.

items.p: A family puts their bottle garden in hot afternoon sun on the balcony. After two days the plants look cooked. What went wrong?
opts: They had too little water
The jar got far too hot inside in the direct sun
The plants ran out of light
items.why: A closed jar in direct sun traps heat, so the air inside gets far hotter than the room. Plants need light, but not that much heat. That is why the Closed Box Test and the Bottle Garden stay in a bright place out of direct sun.

items.p: If the closed box were perfectly sealed and kept in the dark, the seedlings would keep growing for months.
items.why: False. In the dark, the seedlings cannot make food or oxygen. They would use up the food stored in the seeds and the oxygen in the box, and then die. Light is the one thing a closed world must get from outside.

items.p: The Earth has no glass lid. So what keeps Earth's air and water from floating off into space?
items.a: Earth's gravity pulls the air and the water towards the Earth and holds them close, like a lid that you cannot see.
items.why: A strong answer names gravity, the Earth's pull.

items.p: Sort these care actions: does each one send less out of the home, or clean up after it has gone out?

items.why: Sending less out stops the problem at the start. Cleaning up deals with it later. Both help, but sending less out is often easier.

items.p: In the Drain Test, the 'a little' cup grew almost as well as the plain one, but the 'a lot' cup did not. What does this tell us about how much soap matters?
items.a: A small amount of soap made little difference, but a large amount stopped many seeds sprouting. So the amount matters: a little soap spread through a lot of water may do little harm, but a lot of soap in one place harms living things.
items.why: A strong answer uses the results to say that the amount, not just the soap, decides the harm.

items.p: Draw a picture of the Earth as a closed box. Show the sunlight coming in, heat going out, and water going round between sea, cloud, rain and river.

items.a: The Earth with arrows of sunlight coming in, wavy arrows of heat going out to space, and a loop of arrows for water.
items.why: A strong drawing shows what comes from outside (sunlight) and what stays and goes round (water).

items.p: Which of these is the best evidence that the seedlings in the closed box were using the same water again and again?
opts: The seedlings were green
Drops formed on the lid every day and ran back to the cotton, and the box weighed almost the same
The box was clear
items.why: Drops forming on the lid and running back down show the water moving round inside the box. The box weighing almost the same also shows that hardly any water left. Green seedlings alone do not show where their water came from.

items.p: Saalumarada Thimmakka of Karnataka, with her husband, planted and cared for 385 ____ trees along a road.
items.why: She and her husband, Bikkala Chikkaiah, planted the banyans along about 4 km of road between Hulikal and Kudur, and watered them for years. She was given the Padma Shri in 2019.

items.p: Biosphere 2 was meant to be a closed world, like our closed box. Write one thing the closed box test and Biosphere 2 both show about living in a closed world.
items.a: In a closed world, nothing new comes in except light. So what the living things use up or give out stays inside and changes things for everyone there. In the box, water went round. In Biosphere 2, the oxygen used by the microbes was not replaced.
items.why: A strong answer finds something that is true of both, and gives an example from each.

items.p: Put these events from Biosphere 2 in the order they happened.
items: fresh oxygen is pumped in, in 1993
eight people are sealed inside in 1991
scientists find the microbes and the concrete were the cause
the oxygen slowly falls for over a year
a: eight people are sealed inside in 1991
the oxygen slowly falls for over a year
fresh oxygen is pumped in, in 1993
scientists find the microbes and the concrete were the cause
items.why: The oxygen fell first, then oxygen had to be added for the people's safety, and the causes were worked out by careful measuring.

applications: Sewage treatment plants clean a city's waste water with screens, settling tanks and microbes, before it goes back to a river or the sea.
The East Kolkata Wetlands clean much of Kolkata's sewage in fish ponds, where sunlight, algae and microbes do the work.
Tamil Nadu made rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings in 2003, so rain soaks back into the ground instead of running off into drains.
India's Solid Waste Management Rules of 2016 ask every home to keep wet, dry and hazardous waste apart, so each can be treated in the right way.
Space stations recycle water: the International Space Station turns astronauts' breath, sweat and urine back into drinking water.
Bottle gardens, also called terrariums, are kept in homes and offices because a closed one needs very little watering.
Air quality stations in Indian cities measure the air every hour and give it a number, the Air Quality Index (AQI).
Cities restore old lakes, such as the eris of Chennai and the keres of Bengaluru, by stopping sewage and clearing their inlets.
Compost centres run by city corporations turn wet waste from homes into compost for parks and farms.

open_questions.q: How long can a sealed bottle garden live?
open_questions.why_open: Some have lived for decades, like David Latimer's. Nobody knows the limit. It depends on whether the microbes keep turning dead leaves back into food for the plants.

open_questions.q: Can people build a sealed home that keeps them alive for years, on the Moon or on Mars?
open_questions.why_open: Biosphere 2 needed fresh oxygen after about a year and a half. Teams in Russia and China have since kept people for months in sealed homes, but food or supplies still came from outside.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of microbes live around us?
open_questions.why_open: A pinch of soil holds thousands of kinds of bacteria. Most have never been grown in a lab or given a name, so nobody knows how many there are.

open_questions.q: Where does most of the plastic that reaches the sea end up?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists find much less plastic floating on the sea than they expect. Some sinks, some breaks into tiny pieces, and some washes onto beaches. How much goes where is still being measured.

open_questions.q: How much dust from space lands on the Earth each day?
open_questions.why_open: Different ways of measuring give answers from a few tonnes to over a hundred tonnes a day. Either way, it is tiny next to the Earth.

maths.problem: In the Closed Box Test, the open box weighed 120 grams on day 1 and 82 grams on day 7. How many grams of water left the open box?
maths.explain: Take the day 7 weight from the day 1 weight. 120 take away 80 is 40. 40 take away 2 more is 38. So 38 grams of water evaporated into the room's air.
maths.context: This is about the Closed Box Test. You weigh both boxes on day 1 and day 7 to see whether any water left them.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the two weights tells us exactly how much water left, which our eyes cannot measure.

maths.problem: Look at the kitchen scale. Each big mark is 10 grams and each small mark is 2 grams. The pointer is 1 small mark past 110. What does the closed box weigh?
maths.explain: The pointer has passed the 110 mark by one small mark. Each small mark is 2 grams. 110 + 2 = 112.
maths.context: This is about weighing the closed box in the Closed Box Test.
maths.why_maths: A closed box changes weight only a little, so we must read the small marks to see the change.

maths.problem: In the Drain Test, 10 seeds were put in each cup. 10 sprouted in plain water, 9 in 'a little' soap and 4 in 'a lot'. How many more seeds sprouted in plain water than in 'a lot'?
maths.explain: 10 take away 4 is 6. So 6 more seeds sprouted in plain water than in the cup with a lot of washing powder.
maths.context: This is about the Drain Test. You put moong seeds on cotton wet with plain water, a little soapy water or a lot of soapy water, and count how many sprout.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart lets us see at a glance which cup did best, and subtracting tells us by how much.

maths.problem: Farhan's family counted plastic bags brought home: 4 on Monday, 3 on Tuesday, 1 on Wednesday, 0 on Thursday and 0 on Friday. How many bags did they bring home in the 5 days?
maths.explain: Add the days: 4 + 3 = 7, 7 + 1 = 8, and 0 + 0 adds nothing. So 8 bags in 5 days, and none on the last two days, once they carried a cloth bag.
maths.context: This is about Our Family's Care Week. You choose one change and keep a tally each day to see whether it works.
maths.why_maths: A tally each day shows whether a change is really working, instead of guessing.

roots.context: We have looked at the living and non-living parts of our environment, and at the closed box where the same water went round. Now we ask what it means to share one world.

deep_truth.truth: Your open box got lighter as its water evaporated, but that water did not vanish. It went into the air of your room, and in time out to the clouds. Earth is like your closed box: sunlight comes in, and the same water and air go round. So whatever we throw away stays somewhere in the world we all share.
deep_truth.habit: We say we throw things 'away' or wash them 'away', as if they leave the world. Out of sight feels like gone. But the water from the open box, the rasam down the sink and the wrapper in the bin all stay on Earth, somewhere else.
deep_truth.evidence: The open box dried out and got lighter, while the room's air took its water. The closed box kept drops on its lid all week and stayed almost the same weight, because its water could not leave.

three.who_am_i: About two-thirds of your body is water. That water was once in rivers, clouds and other living things, and it will go back to them.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing takes in water and air from their environment, uses them, and gives them back changed.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth gets light and warmth from the Sun, but keeps almost all its own water and air, held close by gravity.

roots.thread: The same water moves between the sea, the clouds, the rain, the tap, your body and the drain. The air you breathe out is breathed in by plants, and the oxygen they give out is breathed in by you. So every living thing on Earth shares one supply of water and air. What one of us puts into it reaches the others, near and far.

science.text: The total amount of water on Earth stays almost the same. It keeps moving between sea, air, land and living things.
Earth loses a tiny amount of light gas to space and gains some tonnes of space dust each day. Both are tiny next to its air and seas.
Whether people can build a sealed home that keeps them alive for years without help from outside is not yet known.

other_view.view: Things do stay on Earth, but that alone is not the problem. A little waste spread through a lot of water or soil can be broken down safely by microbes. What matters is how much goes where, and whether it is treated. With good treatment plants and recycling, 'away' can be made to work.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was walked through as if at home in a city flat today. Changes made: the Closed Box Test uses takeaway boxes, which are not perfectly airtight, so the closed box is said to weigh almost the same, not exactly the same. Both boxes stand in a bright place out of direct sun, because a closed box in hot sun can cook the seedlings. The open box may take longer to dry in cool or rainy weather, so the step says to keep checking until there is a clear difference. Whole moong is used because it sprouts within a day; split dal will not. The tree activity is marked 'if you have a park or a tree nearby', since many flats have none.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1991, eight people walked into Biosphere 2, a huge sealed glass building in the desert of Arizona, USA. Inside were a small rainforest, a desert, a little sea, farm plots and animals. The doors were shut for two years. The planners thought the plants would make all the oxygen the people needed, so the air would stay the same. They were wrong. Month by month, the oxygen fell, until people felt tired and breathless. In January 1993, fresh oxygen had to be pumped in. Scientists, among them Jeff Severinghaus, measured the gases carefully. They found that the soil, full of rich compost, held huge numbers of microbes. The microbes breathed oxygen as they broke down the compost. They should have made extra carbon dioxide, but it went missing too. The bare concrete walls had taken it up. In a closed world, even the soil and the walls are part of the environment.
how_we_found_out.who: The eight people of the first Biosphere 2 mission, among them Jane Poynter and Linda Leigh, and the scientist Jeff Severinghaus
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The planners thought that plants alone would keep the air in a sealed world steady. Careful measuring showed that soil microbes were using up oxygen faster than the plants made it, and that the concrete walls were taking up carbon dioxide.
